title: The call for an agentic standard: We need to stop shipping the same form four different times
text:
The call for an agentic standard: We need to stop shipping the same form four different times

Every assistant draws its own way, and the bill lands on the people who already maintain your button component. This is a call to arms to fix this.

Connecting was the easy part and the plumbing is close to settled for MCP Servers, which followed the lead of HTTP dressed up for the AI era.

What isn’t is what each client does when your agent needs a date picker on screen: which components exist, who owns the rendering, what it looks like when it shows up on a screen.

There are four ways a client can do it, and every product you care about sits in one of them. Nobody publishes that comparison, so sorting out which client does which took four specifications, a protocol proposal and a Google engineering post, and none of them agree on what to call any of it.

Google’s trying to create that standard — A2UI. It’s short for agent-to-UI, their attempt at a shared approach i.e. doing the right thing.

Introduced in December 2025, it is declarative: the agent sends JSON naming components the client already holds in a catalog, and the client draws them in its own code. No markup crosses the wire, and no styling either.

Version 1.0 is still a release candidate and it looks a lot like the HTML constructs of 1999. It matters because it is the one proposal on the table that no vendor “owns.”

Working this out should not be a research project, and this is a call to arms to get there.

Here’s where we are today with A2UI and its adoption.

A2UI

Declarative JSON, rendered by the client

The agent names components the client already holds, and nobody owns the vocabulary. Three apps render it without a bundled renderer, which means they are hedging their bets.

  • Google Gemini Enterprise renders the standard A2UI component set. Styling is Google’s.
  • Google Opal draws its natural-language mini-apps with it. Styling is Opal’s.
  • OpenClaw Canvas renders agent-built UI on connected devices. Styling belongs to the plugin.

A developer tier renders it too — Google’s ADK Web, the alpha Flutter GenUI SDK, CopilotKit AG-UI, Vercel json-render — but nobody works there.

Sandboxed HTML, if you ship the A2UI renderer yourself

A page arrives and runs in a frame. More expressive, less governable, and it stays a web object wherever it lands. These clients do render A2UI: the server sends application/a2ui+json and the app parses it locally with a bundled renderer, which means they are also hedging their bets. Google published three patterns for combining the two in June 2026.

  • OpenAI ChatGPT renders app UI through the Apps SDK. Styling is yours — you shipped the CSS.
  • Anthropic Claude renders Artifacts and hosts MCP Apps carrying their own renderer. Styling is yours, same reason.

Not A2UI List

Declarative JSON through vendor catalog

Same mechanism, one owner.

  • Microsoft Teams and Outlook render Adaptive Cards across seven renderer SDKs. Styling is Microsoft’s, set by host config.
  • Salesforce Slack renders Block Kit. Styling is Slack’s — its docs say Slack controls contrast so you don’t have to.

Generated code or nothing

The model writes the interface fresh each time, or the client has no surface at all.

  • Google Gemini Consumer, writes generative UI per prompt. Styling is whatever the model invented that minute, if at all.
  • xAI Grok renders nothing. It has tools and no surface format at all.

The only approach that lets your server control appearance is the one that ships a page, and that’s the one that turns into a webview on a phone. Every declarative option hands styling to the client, which is a feature right up until the client belongs to somebody else.

Two more things fall out.

  • The declarative approaches are one mechanism with different owners, which is why the model was never the argument.
  • A2UI reaches the clients your users actually open only by shipping its renderer inside every payload — the adapter tax in miniature, and a strange thing to call a standard.

You will pay for that gap. Not in licensing — in a tax. Every surface is another target your design system has to serve, and every platform multiplies it again.

Surfaces times platforms — that’s the surface tax.

Learn from the browser wars

Netscape and Microsoft spent the late 1990s shipping tags at each other. document.layers against document.all.

Every serious site carried browser-sniffing code at the top and two layouts underneath, and the people who wrote that code hated it. Ask Jeffrey Zeldman, which I covered in this article — Designing with web standards: The playbook for this AI moment.

Then Internet Explorer 6 won and the web stopped moving for five years. Firefox pulled developers back by rendering to spec. Google Chrome arrived in 2008 and finished the job — fast, yes, but mostly predictable. You could write a page once and know what it would do. Chrome now holds close to 68% of the browser market, per Statcounter’s July 2026 figures, so it’s a solved problem.

Agentic UI are the old browsers in a new costume, and they are called ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and Slack, with a side of Grok and Perplexity.

The authors of MCP Apps, an extension to the Model Context Protocol, say so in their proposal — without a standard, “developers must maintain separate implementations or adapters for different hosts.” MCP-UI, the project that spec grew out of, counts Postman, Hugging Face, Shopify and ElevenLabs among its adopters. The adapters exist.

Someone is paying for them — it’s us.

Look past chat to the canvas

A message list with an input and a stop button is a solved shape, drawn about the same way everywhere. The canvas is where it gets expensive — Gemini’s Dynamic View, ChatGPT’s Canvas, Microsoft rendering app UI in Copilot chat and out into Teams, Outlook, Word and Excel.

In Google’s own November 2025 evaluation of that generated UI, sites built by human experts still came out on top, and generation can take “a minute or more.”

Runtime assembly needs a shared parts list. Right now every vendor keeps their own.

So Google runs both approaches at once — open-ended code generation in the consumer app, a declarative catalog in the protocol. A consumer canvas can afford a minute and a look it invented this morning. Your product cannot. An approval form on your canvas has to be your date picker, your error states, your empty state, and it has to land before the user’s attention does.

Copy what Slack and Microsoft already proved

The standards argument keeps skipping this. It was solved twice already, in production, by companies with no idea they were prototyping agent UI.

Slack’s Block Kit is blocks, block elements and composition objects, authored as JSON. A server sends the structure; Slack draws it. It runs across messages, modals and App Home tabs, with limits that tell you it’s a real system under load — 50 blocks per message, 100 in a modal.

Microsoft’s Adaptive Cards went further. The pitch is nearly word for word what A2UI now promises: “platform-agnostic snippets of UI, authored in JSON, that apps and services can openly exchange.” Microsoft maintains seven renderer SDKs — JavaScript, .NET, .NET WPF, .NET HTML, Windows UWP, Android and iOS — with React Native contributed by the community.

Teams alone documents a whole card taxonomy: hero, thumbnail, list, connector, adaptive in the same way design systems are documented.

Nobody has to prove declarative UI works across native clients. Microsoft shipped that proof years ago.

The model is not the risk.

The problem is ownership. Block Kit draws in Slack. Adaptive Cards draw in Microsoft’s products. Both are proprietary, and neither will ever be the format the other adopts. If you have ever fought a Block Kit layout into your brand, you know the ceiling of a parts bin somebody else owns.

Make the baseline neutral

A2UI is that baseline, or the best attempt so far. Its 1.0 specification defines surfaces, components and catalogs as JSON naming parts the client already holds — Google calls it a “declarative data format, not executable code.” Same shape as an Adaptive Card, except no vendor owns the parts bin and it streams, so the interface builds as the agent thinks.

Compare that to the other direction. MCP Apps delivers text/html;profile=mcp-app into a sandboxed iframe. That's a page, not a description, and it never becomes a SwiftUI sheet or a Jetpack Compose bottom sheet — on a phone you get a webview, with the wrong scroll physics, the wrong keyboard, Dynamic Type ignored and a VoiceOver reading order from a different document than the one around it. Bundling an A2UI renderer inside that page gets the vocabulary back, not the native widgets.

A component that doesn’t exist in your system cannot appear at all.

The declarative side inverts all of that. A component that doesn’t exist in your system cannot appear at all, an easier promise to make to a security team than “the sandbox will hold.” A2UI’s community renderer list covers SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, React Native, Vue and Lynx — the same native-renderer play Adaptive Cards made, minus the owner.

Version 1.0 stripped theme properties out of the payload entirely, so a button carries a primary variant and nothing about color. Christine Vallaure's UX Collective piece puts the designer's half plainly: the intelligence decides what to show, your design system decides what it looks like. That holds only where the catalog is yours.

The caveat: most of those mobile renderers are volunteer work, and A2UI’s documentation tells you to check compatibility yourself. Microsoft staffs seven of its eight.

Add up the surface tax

Do the multiplication: Your design system probably serves the web, iOS and Android today. Add ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot across Teams and Outlook, and Slack.

Ten surfaces across three platforms isn’t 10 problems, it’s the same date picker in Block Kit JSON, again as an Adaptive Card, again for whatever ChatGPT wants, then regression-tested against a matrix nobody staffed.

There’s a rough price on this for mobile already.

A 2026 survey of 267 app development companies by GoodFirms put a mid-level product built natively for iOS and Android at $120,000 to $300,000, against 20% to 40% less to build it once cross-platform, and maintenance adds 15% to 25% of budget every year after. Agent surfaces cost less per unit, but the shape is the same, and you’re adding units faster than you ever added platforms.

It isn’t elegance. It’s who absorbs the complexity, and right now the answer is your design systems team, if you even have one of at all.

Nathan Curtis wrote about balancing platforms in a design system at EightShapes: once a system serves more than one platform, the real work is deciding what’s shared and what’s justifiably different.

Agent surfaces add a twist — you don’t own the renderer, so you can’t decide at all. The cost lands in the drift. Sparkbox’s 2022 design systems survey of 219 practitioners found 37% of maintainers struggling with design-code parity and 16% tracking usage metrics, and that was before AI.

One shared format doesn’t delete the work.

It changes what you maintain from N implementations to one catalog with N renderers, and moves that burden onto the platform vendors, and right now that’s your team.

Pick a target

After all of this, A2UI might not be the one, in same way there were competing standards in 1999.

Version 1.0 is still a release candidate, the repository has no neutral foundation behind it, and every native deployment so far is Google’s own. Google has abandoned better-supported things.

But the shape is right, and we know it because two companies already shipped it. Adaptive Cards proved a JSON card renders as native UI across seven renderer SDKs. Block Kit proved it carries real interaction at scale. Neither can be the standard, because a standard owned by Microsoft is Microsoft’s standard.

So pick your target, and make every vendor answer one question before you build against theirs: which renderers do you ship, on which devices and who maintains them. The ones who can’t answer are asking you to pay the tax for them.

Start with these four moves now and then plan for a new world

  • Count the cells, not the surfaces. Put surfaces down one axis and platforms across the other, then fill in who owns each cell today. The empty cells are your roadmap, and the count turns this into a budget line.
  • Write the catalog, not the screens. Pick the 12 components an agent needs to finish a task in your product — table, form, date picker, confirmation, status, error and empty state — and specify each with its states and constraints, versioned. That asset transfers to whichever format wins. Screens built against one vendor’s surface don’t.
  • Read the Adaptive Cards schema before you design anything. It’s the most mature declarative UI vocabulary in production, and it will tell you in an afternoon which of your components survive translation and which only work because you control the CSS.
  • Test on a mid-range Android phone first, not last. Run your first agent-rendered form on real hardware with TalkBack on and Dynamic Type up. If it only holds together in a desktop browser, you’ve found the ceiling.

The call for an agentic standard: We need to stop shipping the same form four different times was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Design has outgrown the traditional designer
text:
Design has outgrown the traditional designer

Why design education must reconsider the kind of student it imagines.

For decades, design offered artistically inclined students an appealing compromise. They could pursue a practical career without giving up creativity. Someone with visual talent learned typography, composition, color, image-making, and a collection of professional tools. With enough skill, that student could turn artistic ability into commercial work without the uncertainty of pursuing a career as a traditional artist.

That understanding of the designer still influences recruitment and what many aspiring designers expect from the profession. Design is often presented as a field where creative people can produce visually compelling work while building a recognizable career. The appeal is understandable, and generations of exceptional designers entered the profession through exactly that route.

I know this because it’s how my journey began. I was good at drawing, interested in art, and attracted to a profession that offered a practical outlet for my creativity. That foundation served me well, but it would not have been enough for the career I eventually built.

As the profession changed, I learned to code, moved into user experience and interface design, honed my strategic and business thinking, and developed an interest in the ethical and theoretical questions raised by technology. My career evolved because I did not remain confined by the traditional designer persona.

After two decades in professional design and now as a design educator, I see a growing mismatch between that persona and the profession students are preparing to enter. Students who are comfortable producing visual work are not always interested in research, systems, ethics, technology, or the reasoning that precedes a design decision. Those subjects can feel secondary to the creative work they expected to do, even though designers are now routinely responsible for them.

Artistically inclined students still have a place in design, and replacing them with technically inclined students would solve nothing. What matters is whether students are curious about the questions that now surround the artifact, including how it functions, whose interests it serves, and what consequences it produces.

It is easy to blame AI for disrupting the traditional role of the designer, but the profession’s transformation began much earlier— AI has simply made it more visible. Designers increasingly work on digital products that require attention to behavior, navigation, accessibility, technical constraints, business goals, and decisions affecting entire systems. While traditional design has always involved solving problems, the scope of those problems and the designer’s responsibility for addressing them have expanded.

Labor data offers one practical indication of where the profession is moving. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment for graphic designers to decline 2 percent between 2025 and 2035, while employment for web and digital interface designers is projected to grow 6 percent. The agency also expects automated tools, including AI, to make graphic designers more productive and reduce the number of workers needed.

In 2025, the median annual wage for graphic designers was $62,960, compared with $104,000 for web and digital interface designers. Technology-sector salaries may account for part of the difference, but the market's direction is clear. Employers are paying more for designers who can work with digital products, technical systems, user behavior, and product strategy than for those whose expertise is primarily visual. Traditional visual skills still have value, but they no longer command the same demand or economic value on their own.

Hiring research reported by Figma reinforces this broader shift. While visual polish remained important to 58 percent of hiring managers, it was only one capability within a much wider profile. More than 45 percent also identified collaboration, systems thinking, and product strategy as critical, while 73 percent reported increasing demand for proficiency with AI tools and 79 percent for knowledge of AI product design. Employers are not abandoning visual craft. They are seeking designers whose visual ability is joined with technical, strategic, and systemic knowledge.

I see the mismatch most clearly when students reach the parts of a project that precede the visual work. They may be eager to design screens but impatient with research, resistant to technical constraints, or inclined to treat strategy as documentation to complete before the real design begins. Technology is sometimes learned well enough to operate but not well enough to question.

These reactions are not simply failures of effort. Many students entered the field expecting a professional outlet for artistic creativity. A discipline increasingly concerned with behavior, systems, evidence, and consequences can feel like a change in the terms of that promise.

Changing the curriculum without changing the recruitment pitch leaves that mismatch intact. Programs that present design primarily as a practical outlet for creativity will attract students who expect creative expression to organize the profession. Their frustration is understandable when the education they encounter reflects the realities of contemporary design rather than the false expectations that brought them to the field.

Design programs should therefore reconsider what they advertise and what they evaluate during admissions. A visual portfolio can remain part of the process without serving as the only meaningful evidence of potential. Applicants could also explain how they understood a problem, considered conflicting needs, or changed a decision after encountering new evidence. An imperfect artifact supported by thoughtful reasoning may reveal more than a polished portfolio organized around personal style.

Recruitment could also extend beyond students who already identify with art. Future designers may come through psychology, computer science, business, sociology, communication, or philosophy because they are interested in behavior, technology, organizations, culture, or ethics. Their entry would expand the design field's capabilities rather than displace its artistic students.

The same shift should appear in teaching and evaluation. Projects could require students to defend consequential decisions rather than merely present finished work. Critiques could examine how they responded to conflicting user, technical, and organizational needs. Capstone projects could include evidence of research, iteration, ethical reasoning, and collaboration alongside the final artifact. This would not diminish visual craft, but it would place craft within the broader judgment contemporary design requires.

The profession needs people who can understand consequences not visible in the final artifact. For example, decisions that make an interface simpler, faster, or more personalized may also transfer control from its user to the system behind it. Designers must understand whose interests those systems represent and what users give up for convenience. Such consequences cannot be judged by looking at the screen alone.

This type of responsibility also explains why design will survive AI—despite all the doom and gloom. Generative systems can produce graphics, layouts, interfaces, and variations with extraordinary speed, reducing the number of people needed for visual production. But producing possibilities is not the same as determining which are worth pursuing. Organizations will still need designers to define the purpose, decide whose needs take priority, evaluate consequences, and accept responsibility for the result.

In this new landscape, creativity also takes on a broader meaning. It can appear in framing a problem, exposing a hidden assumption, reorganizing a system, or deciding not to build a proposed product. A beautiful design artifact may demonstrate exceptional craft while serving a system that should never have existed.

Designers whose primary value comes from operating tools and producing polished artifacts will increasingly compete with systems capable of doing that work. Those who can interpret complex situations, make defensible decisions, work across disciplines, and direct those systems toward worthwhile purposes occupy a less replaceable position.

The future of design education depends on more than revised courses, certificates, and new software. Programs must reconsider the person they imagine when they describe a future designer. Artistic imagination remains valuable, but it must be joined by curiosity about research, technology, systems, and the consequences of design decisions.

title: When Endometriosis Makes My Body Unrecognizable, Perfume Helps Me Reclaim It
text:
When Endometriosis Makes My Body Unrecognizable, Perfume Helps Me Reclaim It

Welcome to Note to Self, Refinery29’s fragrance series exploring perfume beyond the bottle. Through intimate stories and scent memories, we’re unpacking the emotions, experiences, and identities behind the fragrances we wear — and why they can become such a deeply meaningful part of who we are.

Some mornings, it feels like my body has been awake for hours before I have. By the time I catch up, it’s already made a series of executive decisions. I’ll stand in front of my closet wondering why nothing feels right, only to realize it’s not the clothes, but the body wearing them. Yesterday’s jeans suddenly feel optimistic; the dress I’d planned to wear belongs to a version of myself who didn’t show up today. After changing twice, I accept the outfit was never the problem. 

Overnight, there’s a heaviness that wasn’t there before. Bloating has appeared from nowhere, and the kind of fatigue sleep barely touches. That’s the strange thing about endometriosis — a condition where cells similar to those lining the uterus grow elsewhere in the body, causing severe pain among other debilitating symptoms. Not only does it change how your body feels, but it changes your relationship with it. Alongside the agony, the fatigue and hormonal shifts mean I’m constantly being reintroduced to my own body. 

That’s usually the point where I do something that sounds faintly ridiculous until you’ve lived it: I reach for perfume.  

The women finding comfort in scent 

While it doesn’t fix anything, fragrance is one of the few things I still get to choose before my body starts calling the shots. More often than not, it’s Esteè Lauder Bronze Goddess — mine and my mom’s summer scent. It smells like vacations, warm, salty skin, and the version of me that existed before pain became something I had to factor into every plan. I wear it because it reminds me I’m still in there somewhere. 

You see, endometriosis erodes the certainty of knowing myself until my body no longer feels like somewhere I can reliably come home to. So when everything else feels unpredictable, is it any wonder I reach for something that smells like continuity? As it turns out, I’m far from the only person with a chronic illness who’s turned my love of fragrance into something much bigger than a simple spritz. 

For Rioco Green 32, fragrance offers a brief escape when her endometriosis flare-ups make the world feel painfully small. “Scent has an amazing ability to transport you somewhere else,” she tells me. Her ritual begins with Aesop Geranium Leaf Body Oil, a herby, invigorating, and grounding scent that helps her momentarily disconnect from the pain while making her feel as though she’s actively caring for a body that’s asking so much of her. 

For Amie Flynn, 34, wearing perfume is about recognition. During an endometriosis flare-up right before a work meeting, she recalls standing in front of the mirror thinking, This isn’t me; it’s just my symptoms. She reached for Jo Malone Poppy & Barley Cologne, as she always does. “The familiar fragrance gave me a moment to pause and reset,” she tells me. “Instead of focusing on how unwell I felt, I was reminded of who I am beyond my diagnosis.”  

None of us expect perfume to perform miracles. Instead, we all ask remarkably little of it: to remind us of who we were before our symptoms got there first. 

Why perfume is more than just beauty — & the science behind it 

Dr. Sula Windgassen, a health psychologist specializing in chronic illness, says this response is remarkably common: “[With endometriosis], body image can be affected by swollen bellies, confidence reduced by brain fog, and your sense of meaning or value as a person can be obscured by pain. It can feel like you just need to survive,” she says. In this version of life, Dr. Windgassen points out something that makes complete sense to me: “Even these small acts of choice start to carry more weight.” 

I recognize this more than I’d like to admit, even when choosing a perfume starts to feel like a personality trait I’m clinging to. It’s where scent slips beyond beauty altogether. Dr. Windgassen adds, “Routines, bodily states, work and relationships can all shift with chronic illness […], but scent can act as a stable cue when everything else is in flux.” 

There’s also a more scientific side to it. Dr. Windgassen points out that certain scents — most notably lavender, bergamot, and chamomile — can activate the parasympathetic nervous system: “This is the body’s built-in ‘calm down’ setting,” she explains. “It slows heart rate and reduces stress responses before you’ve even had time to talk yourself out of it.” 

Unlike other senses like taste or touch, smell doesn’t go through the brain’s usual editing process. “It goes almost directly from the nose to the olfactory bulb, the amygdala, and the hippocampus — areas responsible for emotion and memory,” explains Dr. Windgassen. That could explain why on the hardest days, something as simple as wearing a fragrance during an endometriosis flare-up can offer a little respite. 

How scent can become a grounding ritual for living with endometriosis

It’s something I know all too well. Choosing a perfume on my most painful days is one of the few things my body and I can still agree on. After speaking to psychologists, I kept coming back to one word: anchor. Not in a poetic, lifestyle sense, but something more literal — a way of not drifting too far from myself. 

This is something Anishka Sooriah, 25, has also experienced. She describes losing herself after endometriosis surgery to remove the tissue growing outside of her uterus. For Sooriah, scent became something entirely archival: “There’s this oud oil that my partner gifted me,” she recalls. “Whenever I wear it now, it pulls me straight back to those early days of the relationship. I miss that version of myself sometimes, before the pain.” 

While the emotional pull of scent is deeply personal, there’s also science behind why certain fragrances can make us feel more like ourselves. Dr. Anna Persaud, a biochemist and CEO of This Works, where fragrance meets wellness, says that while we often think of fragrance as purely aesthetic, it can provide emotional support. “Because fragrance engages both memory and emotion simultaneously, a familiar scent can create an immediate sense of recognition and continuity,” she says, adding, “It becomes a sensory cue that reconnects us with ourselves.” 

During periods of grief, upheaval and illness, Dr. Persaud explains that people often return to fragrances they’ve worn for years because familiarity can do the emotional heavy lifting. “Scent doesn’t just help us remember those experiences,” she explains. “It can help us re-experience some of the [positive] emotions associated with them.” Let’s not get it twisted; the perfume isn’t transporting you elsewhere. Instead, it’s a reminder that you’re still here. 

Chriselle Lim, founder of Phlur, has noticed that this shift is now influencing purchasing behaviors. “People are wearing fragrances for themselves rather than other people,” she tells me, adding, “Choosing and applying a scent creates a small sense of normalcy and control.” Lim suggests choosing by mood — and there’s a knack to it. Citrus notes, for example, are thought to boost energy, while skin-like musks feel cocooning and comforting, and woody notes have a grounding effect.  

On my shelf, that means Kilian Paris Sunkissed Goddess (ylang ylang and coconut) for extra warmth, Diptyque Fleur de Peau (bergamot and musk) when I need wrapping up a little, Phlur Paradise Nectar (mandarin and pink pepper) to lift my mood, and Miu Miu Fleur de Lait (mango, coconut, and osmanthus flower) on the days I want to borrow some confidence.  

How I use perfume to find my way back to myself

Naturally, my body decided this would be the week to fact-check everything I’ve just said, and I’m in the middle of one of the worst endometriosis flare-ups I’ve had in months. I’ll spend the next five to nine days cancelling plans, measuring time in pain instead of calendars, and missing the woman I was a few days ago.  

Perfume won’t change any of that. It won’t calm the inflammation, shrink the bloating, or give me back the energy that this condition steals. It isn’t a treatment, and it certainly isn’t a cure. But tomorrow morning, before I face another day of this flare, I’ll still reach for the Bronze Goddess. Not because I want to smell nice, but because, for a few seconds, it reminds me that this version of me isn’t the whole story.  

I used to think perfume was the finishing touch. Turns out, on the days I need it most, it’s where I begin.

title: The Case Against Saving Your Favorite Perfume “For Best”
text:
The Case Against Saving Your Favorite Perfume “For Best”

Welcome to Note to Self, Refinery29’s fragrance series exploring perfume beyond the bottle. Through intimate stories and scent memories, we’re unpacking the emotions, experiences, and identities behind the fragrances we wear — and why they can become such a deeply meaningful part of who we are.

I’ve spent most of my life believing that beautiful things were not meant for ordinary days. Growing up working-class, anything that felt like a luxury came with a quiet set of rules: You looked after it. You made it last. You didn’t use it up too quickly, because replacing it wasn’t always an option. As such, a favorite jumper was saved for occasions; a new pair of shoes was kept box-fresh for as long as possible. And perfume — especially perfume — was something to be rationed.

​The bottles I received for birthdays were some of the most special things I owned. They felt grown-up and extravagant, a little glimpse into a life where I could buy things I loved without worrying about the cost. But because they were so precious, every spray became a decision. I used to think: Was today really worth using it?

Then my aunt died.

While clearing out her belongings, we opened her wardrobe and found bottles of her favorite perfumes: Cacharel Anaïs Anaïs and Nina Ricci L’Air du Temps — all unopened, waiting.

I can’t explain exactly why that sight affected me so much. On the surface, they were just bottles of fragrance, but they represented something much bigger: all of the little pleasures we postpone while waiting for a day that feels more worthy — the celebrations we imagine are coming or the version of ourselves that finally deserves to use the “good” things.

My mom looked at those untouched bottles and said something I’ve never forgotten: “You see, this is why you should never save anything. Wear everything, as it matters — like it’s your last day. Even if it’s just for going to the store. You love it, so you wear it.”

That last sentence has stayed with me ever since, because the more I thought about those unopened bottles, the more I realized my aunt’s perfume wasn’t just about fragrance — it was about all the things we put off enjoying until we believe we’ve earned them. Since then, I’ve found myself questioning why we are so quick to save things that bring us joy. Why does a favorite perfume feel too special for Monday morning? Why do we wait for birthdays, holidays, and big occasions before allowing ourselves to enjoy something we already love?

Jessie Wilner, founder of Discothèque fragrances, helped me put it into words: “We’re conditioned to save [things] for important occasions because modern life is modeled around these supposedly seismic events,” she tells me. Sure enough, friends say they have bottles they only wear for weddings, anniversaries, or vacations. One admitted she’d owned the same expensive bottle for years because she was saving it for something “important.” Another said she kept hers in its original box so it would stay as “pristine” as possible. My sister-in-law has a Diptyque Figuier candle she was given for her 30th birthday that she still hasn’t lit. Whenever I ask why, she just says, “It’s too good to light.”

Likewise, I used to fiercely guard my birthday perfume with my life. One year, it was Prada Paradoxe — all tangerine, jasmine, and warm musk — sprayed so sparingly I almost counted every spritz. The next year: Issey Miyake L’Eau d’Issey, with its watery lotus, fresh lilies, and soft woods; then Estée Lauder Bronze Goddess, with creamy coconut, tiare flower, and vanilla. Each one felt like proof that I had been given something extravagant, and I treated it accordingly: special outfits, special plans, special moods only. But this, says Wilner, means we forget to romanticize the condition of existence. In an increasingly tough world, that matters more than ever.

I understand the thought process. Maybe it comes from growing up without much to spare or the way we’re taught to protect expensive things, to preserve luxury, to keep them untouched for a moment that feels important enough. When money is tight, using something luxurious can feel oddly irresponsible, as if every spray needs to be justified. Even now, with what I think of as “adult money”, I still catch myself calculating whether my Christian Dior Bois Talisman or Diptyque Orpheon is worth wearing for a supermarket trip or a day spent working from home. 

Elodie Durande, perfumer at Ffern, thinks many of us have been conditioned to believe expensive things should only be enjoyed occasionally. The idea of treating perfume as something precious goes back generations. Historically, fragrance was used in religious practices and as a marker of wealth and status. While perfume has become more commercialized, it’s still often treated as something to be saved. “Perfume is such a luxury item, and there’s only a finite amount that comes in a bottle,” Durande tells me. Sure enough, Scento reports that luxury perfume prices rose sharply globally between 2020 and 2025, with raw materials, marketing, and packaging all contributing to higher costs. If you can afford these luxuries, though, Durande says that they deserve to live in the present: “To get the best of them, you need to use them, and enjoy the experience.”

She also raised something I hadn’t considered: the notion that pleasure must be earned. “I think sometimes we feel we need to work to deserve life’s luxuries,” she says, but she also asks, “If you’re always saving something special for when you go out, are you wearing it for others [or] for yourself?”

That question lingered long after the conversation ended. I realized I’d been saving perfume for the moment I felt most presentable and impressive; working from home had only made it easier to convince myself there was no point wearing it at all. But as Wilner says, “Scents are just another way to connect with yourself and others. They don’t have to mark the moments that matter; they can be part of what makes them matter.” Left untouched on a shelf, it’s just liquid in a glass. Worn on an ordinary morning, though, it becomes part of a memory, a mood, and a version of yourself moving through the day.

Sarah McCartney, perfume enthusiast and founder of curated fragrance store Soliflore, tells me she sees this realization in customers all the time: “The right moment is today,” she says. “We can’t predict tomorrow, and there’s no guarantee a special occasion will come along that feels worthy enough. If a fragrance makes you feel confident, comforted, or simply happy, then that’s reason enough to wear it.” The joy comes from wearing it, not collecting it, says McCartney, which is the exact opposite of the mindset I’d grown up with, but one I’m learning to embrace.

Eudora Nwasike, a certified fragrance specialist and content creator, arrived at the same conclusion through a much more personal experience. After her father passed away in 2022, she talks about one of the greatest lessons he left her with — to never wait for a special occasion. “Every waking day counts as a special occasion, because nothing in life is promised,” she tells me. “Don’t deny yourself little pockets of joy in a rough world. Wear your fragrances, expensive or affordable.” Her favorites include Amouage Purpose Eau de Parfum, plus the more affordable Zara Fashionably London Elixir Parfum and Phlur Cherry Stem Eau de Parfum, to name a few.

Certainly, there’s some science behind those little pockets of joy, too. One recent study found that pleasant fragrances may boost positive emotions and improve social interactions. Another study found that certain scents, such as lavender and ylang-ylang, could enhance mental performance and focus. With that in mind, ​my Jo Malone Sea Salt & Bergamot Cologne now sees the grocery store aisles. Discothèque’s Baise Moi on The Dancefloor comes with me on dog walks. Acqua di Parma Rosa Nobile has accepted that each spritz now includes emails, errands, and occasionally standing in the kitchen wondering what to make for dinner.

So I’ll leave you with a very small act of rebellion: I’m no longer saving anything for best. Now, every spritz of the fragrance I own feels like a small act of gratitude, a reminder to use what I love while I’m here to enjoy it. Perhaps that’s the lesson my aunt taught me without ever knowing it: the things we love aren’t meant to be preserved for a life that hasn’t happened yet. They’re meant to be part of the one we have now.

title: The 5 Fragrance Trends Set To Define Fall, According To A Master Perfumer
text:
The 5 Fragrance Trends Set To Define Fall, According To A Master Perfumer

If the name Alberto Morillas doesn’t immediately ring a bell, the names on his impressive CV certainly might. Calvin Klein CK One, Gucci Bloom, Marc Jacobs Daisy, Flower by Kenzo — these are perfumes we’ve all encountered in one way or another, whether they’ve taken pride of place on your own perfume shelf, remind you of a loved one’s signature scent, or inspired a fleeting spritz at the department store, hoping you’d come back one day and finally make the purchase.

In other words, what Morillas — now the founder of his own perfume brand, Mizensir — doesn’t know about perfume probably isn’t worth knowing. Which makes him particularly well placed to predict the biggest and most interesting fragrance trends for the seasons ahead. And what’s that? A slight chill in the air? Whether you’re hankering for pumpkin spice or hanging on to the last days of sunshine, fall is right around the corner, and with it comes a whole new laundry list of notes, accords, and ways to wear your fragrance.

Ahead, Morillas predicts the top perfume trends to watch this fall, and how to make them work for you.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Bitter & Dark Notes

Gourmand fragrances — perfumes with edible, dessert-like notes — are everywhere you turn, but Morillas predicts that this fall, we’ll have had our fill of strawberries, caramel, and Chantilly cream. “These notes are quite simple,” Morillas says, “but a perfume with true depth features a slight bitterness to it.” This is why fragrance brands are leaning towards slightly more unusual notes. “Think artichoke, herbs like thyme, grass such as vetiver, and plants like cypriol,” says Morillas — all of which add a herbaceous, mysterious edge to counteract the saccharine sweetness of popular notes like vanilla.

Creed’s Wild Vetiver Eau de Parfum boasts grassy vetiver and zingy pink pepper to balance the lush rose and syrupy berries. Then there’s Mizensir Mythique Vetyver, with vetiver, Sicilian lemon, and geranium bourbon — a leafy, green rose. If you have less to spend, try Le Monde Gourmand Santal Supreme, with green vetiver, skin-like musk, and sweet, powdery violet.

Pre-Scenting Your Clothes

Having a perfume base layer — like using a scented body wash or body lotion — before applying fragrance is nothing new, and can help you smell better for longer. But Morillas thinks most of these products smell pretty ordinary. If you’ve found a perfume you really love and want to maximize its sillage — the scent cloud that follows you around all day — Morillas recommends scenting your wardrobe.

It’s as simple as investing in a porcelain or ceramic hanging ornament, spritzing your favorite fragrance all over it, then placing it inside your wardrobe so the scent molecules gradually infuse the fabric of your clothes, enhancing your overall scent. It pays to choose fragrances with excellent staying power, anyway. I love Mizensir Ylang Spirit, with warm, solar notes of jasmine, vanilla, and bergamot. Also try R29 Fragrance Award 2026 winners: Diptyque Orphéon Eau de Parfum, with gin-like juniper berries and vanilla-esque tonka bean, and Byredo Future Memories Eau de Parfum, a smorgasbord of clean orange blossom, rich vanilla liquor accord, and tart blackcurrant.

If you really want to infuse your threads, opt for an extrait de parfum — one of the highest fragrance concentrations.

Burnt Notes

Bonfires? In fall? Groundbreaking. But smoky woods, charred cedar, and a hint of burnt embers are pretty revolutionary in fragrance, according to Morillas, who predicts that the creamy, green woods we know and love in fragrances like Phlur’s Father Figure and Refinery29 Fragrance Award 2026 winner Maya Njie Nordic Cedar are taking on a toasted effect this season.

“Fire notes are not easy to capture because there’s so much nuance,” says Morillas. “Smoke, burning embers, and ash all have different smells,” he continues, “but they’re perfect for fall because they’re so cocooning.” There’s also a danger element to them, adds Morillas, which makes them exciting.

AllSaints Naked Woods opens with verdant notes of tart apple and freshly picked rhubarb — green leaves and all — but dries down to something warm and cozy thanks to amber woods, which smell richer and darker than green, creamy woods like cedar. Also try Kilian Paris Midnight Espresso Eau de Parfum, with coffee, hazelnut, and rum, which lend a roasted edge, and Cyklar Amber Hour, a combination of amber resin, singed palo santo, and vanilla-like tonka bean.

The Apothecary Effect

Basil, fresh herbs, and minty notes are making their way into fragrance, bringing the same easy appeal they have in food, says Morillas. He describes them as “simple pleasures” in both taste and scent: fresh, uplifting and familiar. Just as a handful of herbs can transform a simple dish, they can give a fragrance an instant lift, adding a hit of freshness and vibrancy — a welcome antidote to fall and winter’s greying skies.

Try Olfactory X Mint + Apricot Eau de Parfum, with basil and mint alongside sun-warmed apricot, tangy blackcurrant, and syrupy dates. We also love Uni’s Sunset Water-Based Perfume, an aromatic mix of crushed mint and zingy lemon with grassy patchouli and smoked sandalwood. Then there’s ‘Ôrəbella WINDOW2SOUL Parfum, where fresh mint slices through heady damask rose and jasmine.

Cool Musks

The musk perfumes we all know and love have a distinct skin-like quality to them, reminiscent of stepping out of a warm bath or pulling on a loved one’s well-worn sweater. But there’s a new musk in town, says Morillas — and instead of skin, it smells like the great outdoors: crisp air, cool greenery, and freshly cut grass.

“I call these ‘cool’ musks,” says Morillas. “It’s hard to capture the sensation of coolness,” he adds, “but we do this by including one particular note: camphor.” A waxy substance derived from the camphor laurel tree, camphor is often used in chest rubs thanks to its medicinal, cooling, and invigorating qualities — which, in fragrance, translates to that elusive sensation of icy coolness.

There’s a dash of this in Ellis Brooklyn’s DEAR SKY Eau de Parfum (think pink pepper, honeydew melon, and zippy bergamot), Yves Saint Laurent Libre Berry Crush Eau de Parfum (creamy coconut, soothing lavender, and juicy raspberry), and Givenchy Very Irresistible Eau de Parfum (spicy star anise, sprightly blackberry, and buttery vanilla).

Scenting Your… Hands

Lastly, your hands are one of the most underrated places to wear fragrance, hints Morillas. Think scented hand sanitizer or a fragrant hand cream, then bring the scent up over your wrists and onto the backs of your hands. It makes sense. We use our hands constantly — typing at our keyboards, reaching for our phones, running our fingers through our hair — so every movement creates a little burst of fragrance. It’s also one of the easiest ways to enjoy your own perfume throughout the day, rather than leaving an obvious scent trail for everyone else.

No one does scented hand cream better than Cyklar. Try Sacred Santal, which smells like an enchanted woodland while packing urea and ectoin — two seriously moisturizing ingredients that help keep hands soft and smooth. Then there’s Salt & Stone’s Bergamot & Hinoki Nourishing Hand Cream, formulated with hydrating niacinamide and softening seaweed extract. And one of our favorites, which needs no introduction: Glossier You Hand Cream.

title: What I Think About When I Choose How I Smell As A Trans Woman
text:
What I Think About When I Choose How I Smell As A Trans Woman

Welcome to Note to Self, Refinery29’s fragrance series exploring perfume beyond the bottle. Through intimate stories and scent memories, we’re unpacking the emotions, experiences, and identities behind the fragrances we wear — and why they can become such a deeply meaningful part of who we are.

What’s in a name? That which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet.”

When I came out as trans in 2017, this well-known Shakespeare line held a lot of meaning as I chose my name. Overlooked by so many, our names are an important part of our identity, and as a trans woman, hearing people use mine — like external acceptance of my authentic self — was incredibly affirming. But in hindsight, I missed something important in that quote: the sense of smell.

You see, the fragrances we choose are just as integral to our identities as our monikers. Patchouli, ylang-ylang, cedar, and so many other names belonging to notes of a different type from the ones I recognized as a musician now jumped out at me as I found ways to express myself.

Before I came out, the fragrances I bought were as gender neutral as possible. It was my way of avoiding masculinity and being able to secretly embrace who I really was. After coming out, an entirely different world was unlocked, and I quickly realized that changing my fragrance was just as exciting, not to mention cathartic, as updating my wardrobe.

I was on a mission to find my style and a scent that encapsulated that. Was I sweet? Perhaps floral? Or was I something bolder? The first fragrance I bought was Katy Perry’s Mad Love, sadly now discontinued. It was a light, fruity, and playful fragrance that allowed me to express my femininity in a fun way, at a time in my life when I was finding ways to show up in the world — even if that did involve some questionable outfit choices. Most importantly, it was affordable. As a trans woman, I was condensing years of “growing up” into months, on top of everyday adult life. While the cis women I knew were able to experiment and refine their style in their younger years, I was on an Instagram-fueled crash course in makeup and style; I wasn’t ready to splash out on fine fragrance just yet.

As it turns out, I wasn’t the only one who felt a need to balance cost with an existing connection. Journalist Sophie Layton, 23, tells me, “My first fragrance was a SO…? body spray; I think it was Wild Berries. I had decided I wanted to start with that brand because it was one that my best friend (and basically big sister) used herself, and she played such an important role in my transition, especially in the early days.” It was a good balance of fun but not bank-breaking, says Layton.

After coming out, Summer Healey, 37, regularly jumped at any offers of perfume samples to discover and experiment with notes she liked before settling on Prada Paradoxe Eau de Parfum — a heady bouquet of neroli, jasmine, and orange blossom. “I remember Prada being a brand I always resonated with visually, but smelling that first Paradoxe sample, I was hooked by the soft floral tones that felt like an inner home,” she recalls. Healey continues, “Early transition — even before being out socially — having my scent felt like wearing armour, and smelling it on my wrists made me feel more confident.”

In a society that demonizes us more than it tries to understand us, confidence is everything when taking those steps outside. After all, we go to work, we meet friends, and we walk our dogs just like everyone else, but with an added layer of caution. Even as someone who’s been out for nine years, I’m always looking over my shoulder when I’m out in public, always ready for abuse — or to run. It’s no surprise that how we express ourselves is also influenced by a need for safety. For me, it’s how I present and how I smell, hoping that if a passerby catches the scent of my fragrance, they don’t stop to question who just walked past. It seems Layton agrees: “Being seen to put on body spray definitely helps [with the] perception of others,” she tells me.

On my journey of expression, it’s not just my transness that I’ve learned a lot about. As someone diagnosed with autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (AuDHD), I’ve discovered my sense of smell has been an unwitting co-pilot in my transness and self-expression all along. A smell is either awful and offensive, or it’s amazing and stimulates my brain. There’s no in-between, just full-on intensity. The result has been curating a careful balance of expressive scents that will also help ground me and regulate my mood and emotions.

My latest go-to fragrances are Versace Dylan Purple Eau de Parfum (think juicy pear, effervescent bergamot, and Iso E Super — a molecule that smells different on everyone), and YSL Black Opium Eau de Parfum (with sweet vanilla, bitter coffee, and airy orange blossom). Both are sweet and joyful but with more distinct, confident notes and more immediate presence. Since my first Katy Perry fragrance, a lot has changed. I’ve grown up, and these fragrances are the latest bookmark in my current chapter of life.

But here’s the thing: I can’t ignore how heavily gendered fragrances can be. We’re practically told what we can or can’t buy, and it’s all in the language brands use to market them. “Daisy, by Marc Jacobs. The fragrance for women” or “Boss Bottled. The Man of Today.” But why can’t men wear sweet, floral fragrances? The answer lies in the same box as why a man wouldn’t dream of ordering a cheeky glass of rosé when on a night out with the boys.

In unpacking my own identity, I was also unpacking the box of gender constructs. Historically, men were perceived as tough and strong, while women were delicate and nurturing, giving rise to the modern stereotypes that hold us back today. Despite concerted attempts as a society to leave these stereotypes behind, the fragrance industry still relies on gendered cues to appeal to us for one simple reason: consumerism. Douglas Little, CEO and founder of Heretic Parfum, a brand that has been pushing the boundaries and perceptions of fragrance, tells me, “For centuries, perfume wasn’t divided into ‘for him’ and ‘for her.’ Scent was ritual, medicine, seduction, power, status.” Take ancient Egypt, where fragrant oils were used in religious practices as well as worn for beauty across genders. Similarly, in ancient Rome, fragrance was often a marker of wealth and social standing.

Little adds, “The idea that a rose belongs to women or leather belongs to men is a remarkably modern invention, one born less from art than from marketing. Once fragrance became a mass-market commodity, it became easier to sell if everything was neatly divided into two aisles.” The irony, says Little, is that scent has no gender: “Vetiver doesn’t know who is wearing it; jasmine isn’t feminine; oud isn’t masculine. These are stories we’ve assigned to raw materials, and after hearing them long enough, we’ve mistaken them for truth.”

But to a certain extent, trans people do embrace gendered cues, and not just for protection. Layton says, “For a lot of people, they’ve spent a significant chunk of their lives being told, ‘You can’t do x, wear y, or use z, because it’s for girls’, so when they come out, doing all of those things that can be considerably feminizing [like] reclaiming that in a way.”

Trans advocate Robyn Newark, 39, tells me, “I’ve had past experiences of hating masculine scented products like shower gel and shaving cream, so changing those to feminine ones feels more affirming and freeing, especially when you’ve previously felt like you exist in a prison of expected gender presentation — including scent.” Certainly, clothing or the length of my hair is an obvious form of outward expression, but I feel it’s more symbolic and doesn’t fully capture just how incredibly personal that reclamation process is.

Personally, fragrance is the key — a feeling that can be applied to any outfit, giving it depth and meaning. “To me, wearing perfume is one of the most intimate acts of self-expression we have,” says Little. “It’s invisible, deeply personal, and impossible to fully explain.” Little adds, “The most heretical thing we can do isn’t create another fragrance; it’s freeing people from the idea that scent needs permission to belong to them.” A fragrance can not only add something to our outfits and to how we feel, but it can also lend itself to moments, too. “Smell is definitely a little bit more for me than for anyone else,” says Newark. “I also enjoy it when engaging in intimate play with others, sometimes choosing to spritz my lower back or lower stomach.”

While fragrance is likely to remain gendered for quite some time, our love/hate relationship with it needn’t be so toxic. After all, it’s easier to find your identity when you know who you’re not, or what you don’t like, right? What some see as preference, I see as meaning. Gendered cues are simply my starting point; non-statutory guidance that I can choose to embrace, or not. Little agrees: “I’ve always believed fragrance should express who you are, not who society expects you to be. At Heretic, we don’t compose perfumes around gender; we compose around emotion, atmosphere and desire. I want someone to choose a fragrance because it makes them feel haunted, dangerous, euphoric, nostalgic, or transformed, not because it was placed on the ‘correct’ shelf.”

As I look at my shelf and the fragrance collection I’ve accumulated over the last nine years, I see far more than something that completes an outfit. Curated by my neurodiversity and my trans identity, I see a timeline. A visual and deeply personal representation of how far I’ve come, with each one unlocking intimate emotions and core memories of my self-discovery. Every spray is a part of my journey that I choose to share with others, all while reminding myself that we are not static beings, but individuals who can redefine boundaries as we continue to grow.

title: I Own Over 300 Perfumes, But These 7 Earn Me The Most Compliments
text:
I Own Over 300 Perfumes, But These 7 Earn Me The Most Compliments

Welcome to Note to Self, Refinery29’s fragrance series exploring perfume beyond the bottle. Through intimate stories and scent memories, we’re unpacking the emotions, experiences, and identities behind the fragrances we wear — and why they can become such a deeply meaningful part of who we are.

If I had to hazard a guess, I’d say I own more than 300 fragrances. As a perfume content creator and certified fragrance specialist, scent is my entire job — and I don’t discriminate. My collection spans everything from niche houses like Ex Nihilo and Initio Parfums to budget-friendly gems (Zara’s fragrances, created in collaboration with Jo Malone, are seriously underrated).

While I have plenty of long-time favorites that I return to despite the constant stream of new launches, only a select few consistently stop people in their tracks. If you ask me, there’s no better feeling than someone complimenting your perfume. It validates your personal taste and leaves a lasting impression long after you’ve left the room.

With that in mind, I wanted to share the handful of fragrances that never fail to turn heads. Whether you’re looking for a new signature scent or want a perfume that people can’t help but ask about, these are the bottles that have proven themselves time and time again — and I’m willing to bet they’ll do the same for you.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Eudora Nwasike (@a.dose.of.e)

DashDividers_1_500x100

Giorgio Armani Stronger With You Powerfully Eau de Parfum

Just when you thought the Stronger With You line couldn’t get any better, Armani dropped its best flanker yet. Stronger With You Powerfully gave me a literal nosegasm. It’s an addictive blend of juicy cherry, smoked chestnut, and rich bourbon vanilla that still stays true to the collection’s signature DNA of warm, smoky vanilla and fresh, herbaceous lavender. If you’re looking for a first-date fragrance that’ll have them leaning in and asking, “What are you wearing?”, this right here is the one.

Zara Fashionably London Elixir Parfum

Out of every fragrance in Zara’s Cities collection — created by Jo Malone CBE, no less — Fashionably London Elixir is the one I keep coming back to. It’s a sweet, airy rose, but nothing like the old-school, powdery florals you might be imagining. Instead, sparkling bergamot and clean, skin-like musk give it a fresh, modern edge. It smells effortlessly sophisticated and, on me, lasts more than eight hours on both skin and clothes. Talk about bang for your buck. If you’re after a bougie-on-a-budget fragrance that’ll work for literally any occasion, any time of year, start here.

Amouage Purpose Eau de Parfum

Amouage Purpose is a modern classic and one that will always have a place in my ever-growing collection. It’s a spicy, smoky, woody fragrance built around frankincense, pimento (yes, the pepper!), sandalwood, and akigalawood, a sustainable molecule derived from patchouli. Whenever I wear it, it never fails to attract compliments. I’m talking, “Wow, you smell unreal,” or “I could smell you before I saw you — I need to know what perfume you’re wearing.” It’s a true projection monster, so a little goes a very long way. The fact that it gets people talking comes as no surprise, since the brand recently took home two wins at the 2026 Fragrance Foundation Awards.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Eudora Nwasike (@a.dose.of.e)

Balmain Carbone Eau de Parfum

Balmain Carbone was composed by one of the most prolific perfumers of our time, Quentin Bisch (think Carolina Herrera Good Girl, Chloé Nomade, and Parfums de Marly Delina), yet it feels incredibly special and unique. If you like fragrances in the realm of Amouage Guidance (creamy, spicy and rich — like an indulgent dessert), Carbone will be right up your street. It’s a beautiful composition of musky suede rose with woody touches that give it a more androgynous edge. Four to six spritzes and the compliments will be rolling in all day.

Phlur Cherry Stem Eau de Parfum

Phlur’s Cherry Stem may not be the most talked-about fragrance in the collection, but if you ask me, it’s seriously underrated. Juicy black cherry meets soft leather and warm caramel, while a subtle boozy edge keeps it from becoming tooth-achingly saccharine. It’s sweet without being sticky, with moderate projection that means you’ll catch those addictive little wafts throughout the day (or night). If you’re new to fragrance or want something that feels effortless and cool without trying too hard, Cherry Stem is the perfect place to start.

Byredo Bal d’Afrique Absolu de Parfum

When I smell this, it instantly transports me to the Caribbean — and I think that’s exactly why people comment on it so much. Who doesn’t want to feel like they’re on vacation every day? Bright bergamot and tart blackcurrant open the fragrance before melting into a delectable praline note, followed by a warm, woody, amber base. Despite the deeper notes, it remains clean, airy, and fresh. I love layering it with Maison Francis Kurkdjian Baccarat Rouge 540 Extrait to amplify the praline’s addictive sweetness.

Frédéric Malle Contre-Jour Eau de Parfum

Contre-Jour may have only launched this year, but it’s already become one of my most complimented fragrances. It was love at first sniff and showcases the beauty and complexity of immortelle, the everlasting flower, in all its honeyed, smoky glory. A generous dose of rose creates a stunning contrast, while soft sandalwood with a subtle herbal edge keeps the composition feeling natural and refined. It’s the kind of fragrance that makes people stop and ask what I’m wearing — not because it announces itself, but because it leaves behind a trail that feels expensive. If I had to describe it in three words, they’d be artistic, complex, and enigmatic. This is a scent for those who appreciate the finer things in life.

title: The R29 Editors’ Guide To Everything Worth Seeing, Doing, & Sampling At Beautycon 2026
text:
The R29 Editors’ Guide To Everything Worth Seeing, Doing, & Sampling At Beautycon 2026

Beautycon is back for 2026, and this September 19, we’re sending you to school. Beautycon University, to be exact, at Rolling Greens LA. But don’t worry, these classes are nothing like the ones you remember. 

Grab your notepad and choose your own curriculum across five beauty “majors” — Art, Business, History, Science, and Wellbeing. Get up close with celebrity makeup artists, in-demand dermatologists, and special guests like Cardi B and Keke Palmer, with study sessions including hands-on masterclasses, creator-led conversations, immersive brand experiences, product discovery, and insider knowledge you won’t find on your FYP. 

With that in mind, here are seven things worth seeing, doing, and sampling (yes, there’ll be swag!) at Beautycon University 2026.  

It’s the one time you won’t want to be saved by the bell. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

A masterclass in technique by Beyoncé’s makeup artist, Sir John 

Fancy yourself as the makeup artist celebrities like Beyoncé, Zendaya, and Naomi Campbell have on speed dial for the biggest dates in their diaries? Then you’ll want to be front row at our Head of School Sir John’s masterclass, where the makeup maestro and creative director will share his most valuable techniques and top tips — plus, as the originator of the viral “dopamine glam” movement, reveal the makeup trends set to dominate the year ahead. 

“It’s a huge honor to step into the role of Head of School this year,” Sir John told R29. “I’m most excited to set the tone for the day, bring the energy, and create an environment where everyone feels excited to jump in and be part of the Beautycon University experience. Ultimately, I want us to connect, celebrate beauty and community, and, most importantly, have a really fun time!”

Cardi B with her hair care brand, Grow-Good Beauty  

From waist-length waves to bold bobs, there isn’t a hairstyle Cardi B hasn’t rocked with confidence, so it’s fair to say she knows a thing or two about caring for her lengths. It makes sense, then, that she has her own hair-care brand — and one we’re particularly fond of at R29. Grow-Good combines classic ingredients (think nourishing avocado, hydrating aloe vera, and shine-enhancing moringa seed) with serious science to help deliver healthier, stronger, better-looking hair. Discover her full product lineup and catch a glimpse of the pop-culture icon herself. Okurr!

Actor, entrepreneur, and Pilates instructor Keke Palmer on how to be strong & well 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Keke™ (@keke)

Beauty and wellness go hand in hand, which is why we’ve enlisted none other than Keke Palmer to lead a one-hour mat Pilates class, Practice by Palmer. Move, stretch, and get your sweat on alongside the multi-hyphenate as she takes you through an energizing workout designed to leave you feeling strong and invigorated. Be sure to register in advance to secure your mat, then stick around to refresh with the beauty and wellness samples on hand. 

The Buseum, aka Beauty Museum 

Step into the Buseum, an immersive installation where history, art, and beauty collide. Journey through the eras with Refinery29 Somos, and discover the iconic Latina beauty trends that have shaped LA culture, beauty, and politics, from the Pachucas to the chola aesthetics of the 1990s. Then, wander through the beautifully curated Fragrance Awards 2026 showcase, a gallery-like celebration of this year’s winning scents, from Phlur’s Vanilla Canyon to Ellis Brooklyn’s Plum Tonic, and take home samples from some of the brands behind them. Who knows? You might just find your next signature scent. 

A live recording of Nose Dive, Refinery29 and eos’ fragrance podcast, with guest Jackie Aina 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Jackie Asamoah (@jackieaina)

We’ve had singer JoJo and fashion editor and stylist Gabriella Karefa-Johnson, and now it’s content creator and entrepreneur Jackie Aina’s turn in the scented seat as we record Nose Dive — Refinery29’s brand-new fragrance-meets-pop-culture podcast — live at Beautycon University. Expect deep chats, cultural commentary, and, of course, plenty of laughs. 

Beauty creator Glamzilla on the secrets to scroll-stopping content 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Stephanie Santana (@glamzilla)

Content creator, beauty extraordinaire, and the internet’s beauty big sister, Glamzilla, aka Stephanie Santana, has had a hand in more makeup trends than we can count — and now she’s bringing her expertise to the Beautycon main stage. Catch her live podcast taping, where she’ll reveal her invaluable tips for creating content that cuts through, plus her secrets to flawless contouring and the perfect lip combo. When it comes to makeup, there’s very little Glamzilla doesn’t know about perfecting a look.

title: Cardi B Is Coming To Beautycon! Here Are 9 Of Her Best Beauty Looks
text:
Cardi B Is Coming To Beautycon! Here Are 9 Of Her Best Beauty Looks

Everyone loves a good Cinderella story. And it feels like Cardi B is Hollywood’s very own rags-to-riches princess now reigning over the industry. She has amassed over 193 million followers across Instagram and TikTok since bursting onto the scene in 2015 — and as the numbers keep boomin’, the beauty is bangin’. Some OG fans remember watching the college student-turned-grocer-turned-stripper’s hilarious Instagram videos back in 2015, where she outlined her sexcapades, her plastic surgery procedures, and anything else you — or she — could imagine. That candor is why we fell in love with her, and it’s why we love all of her looks even more. Cardi B is bringing her signature honesty and her beauty knowledge to Beautycon this year and we can’t wait.

Cardi B’s audience grew by multitudes once she landed a spot on Love & Hip Hop: New York. From there, America fell for the Bronx native’s sharp wit, endless one-liners, and rainbow of colorful hairstyles — and she’s only built on that momentum since. She’s now a mother of four, and continues to make headlines for her music, her personal life, and her impeccable fashion and beauty looks.

As her spotlight has grown brighter, Cardi’s beauty game has only gotten stronger. She’ll still pull a wildcard by throwing on a fiery red, waist-length bussdown or a bright green lip, but she’s also become a bona fide beauty entrepreneur: earlier this year she launched her own haircare line, Grow-Good Beauty, born out of her own struggles with damaged hair. And now, that side of her career is about to hit a major milestone as Cardi B is set to lead a hands-on haircare masterclass at Beautycon University on September 19 in Downtown Los Angeles (get your tickets here!). It’s the perfect stage for a star who’s spent a decade turning her beauty experiments into a full-blown brand. 

To celebrate Cardi B at Beautycon — and the fact that she’s become a beauty mogul in her own right — we’re walking you through her best beauty looks, ahead.

DashDividers_1_500x100

2019: Rainbow Bussdown & Yellow Nails

An unbeatable combo! Cardi B attends the Swisher Sweets Awards at The London West Hollywood on April 12, 2019 in West Hollywood, California, rocking bold pink eye makeup, a rainbow wig and long, bright yellow nails to tie the look together.

2018: Bejeweled Headgear & A Jewel-Toned Beat

Cardi B, looking heavenly, attends the Heavenly Bodies: Fashion & The Catholic Imagination Costume Institute Gala at The Metropolitan Museum of Art on May 7, 2018 in New York City. This iconic look matched vivid liner with rich colors and a deep red lip.

2026: Technicolor Updo & Soft Pink Eyeshadow

Cardi B arriving to Cardi B’s “Little Miss Drama” tour after party on April 08, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania rocking technicolor hair in a beautiful updo and soft eyes to compliment the bold hair.

2026: Sharp Liner & A Diamond Accent

Cardi B attends the 2026 Met Gala Celebrating “Costume Art” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art on May 04, 2026 in New York City. Structured brows, a diamond face jewel, subtle lips, and a beauty look that lets your fit shine? She nailed it.

2024: Drops of Emerald & Matching Shadow

Cardi B attends the 2024 Met Gala celebrating “Sleeping Beauties: Reawakening Fashion” at The Metropolitan Museum of Art on May 06, 2024 in New York City. Rocking all black, Cardi B used her nails, jewelry and bright emerald accents to bring pops of color to the look.

2018: Florals & Fiery Red

Cardi B attends the 2018 American Music Awards at Microsoft Theater on October 9, 2018 in Los Angeles, California. For this beauty look, she leaned into the floral theme and went with bright lips and matching eye shadow.

2016: Very Millennial Eyes & A Nude Lip

Cardi B attends the 2016 VH1 Hip Hop Honors: All Hail The Queens at David Geffen Hall on July 11, 2016 in New York City. This was the makeup look every millennial was rocking in 2016 and we miss it.

2025: A Romantic Fishtail Braid in Paris

Cardi B is seen outside Ashi Studio during the Haute Couture Fall/Winter 2025/2026 as part of Paris Fashion Week on July 8, 2025 in Paris, France. Cardi B may be known for her long, colorful bussdowns, but we loved when she kept it simple and romantic for this look in Paris.

Cardi B attends the Billboard 2018 R&B Hip-Hop Power Players event at Legacy Records on September 27, 2018 in New York City in a highlighter green bob and matching neon liner, reminiscent of Lil Kim in the 90s.

title: Sydney Sweeney’s Favorite Fall Denim Starts With This Y2K Revival Trend
text:
Sydney Sweeney’s Favorite Fall Denim Starts With This Y2K Revival Trend Sydney Sweeney knows what she likes, and it starts with low-rise jeans.

The 28-year-old actress has kept busy, starring in The Housemaid, reprising her role of Cassie in Euphoria season three, and sitting on a slew of unreleased projects. Still, her stacked schedule couldn't keep her away from American Eagle—and for her third collaboration with the brand, she’s once again putting denim at the forefront.

Post the polarizing 2025 “Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans” campaign and this summer’s “Syd for Short” push, the actress is doubling down on her relationship with the brand, starring in a campaign for one of the most nostalgic denim trends. The curated fall lineup includes straight-leg, wide-leg, barrel, and bootcut options, all with one defining detail: a hip-grazing waist. 

“Fashion always comes back around, but I think people are ready to have fun with denim again,” Sweeney exclusively told Refinery29, calling the hipsters an “exciting change” after high-rise jeans dominated the better part of the last decade.

But the low-rise revival isn’t showing up in the same way as it did in the 2000s. Instead of copying and pasting a look from Christina Aguilera’s Dirrty era and wearing overly tight pants, Sweeney is redefining the denim staple with a more relaxed and practical approach, reaching for billowy, classic, and fitted styles alike. “Low-rise isn’t tied to one super-specific silhouette anymore,” she said. 

Sweeney’s reimagined approach shines through the accompanying photoshoot. In one look, Sweeney wears a minimalist white tank top, reaching for a cropped denim jacket in another. In all, she goes barefoot with tousled hair. The styling feels removed from the need to recreate Y2K looks exactly (think butterfly tank tops and platform flip-flops), reminding us that wearing low-rise jeans is extremely personal; it’s less about dressing like the early aughts and more about making the trend your own. For Sweeney, that starts with the fit.

“I know pretty quickly when I put on a pair of jeans whether I’m going to live in them,” she said. Comfort—or a lack thereof—can make or break a pair of pants, which is why finding the right balance between stretch and structure is essential. Thankfully, American Eagle’s fall low-rise collection offers denim that moves with you, without ever sacrificing shape.

Love them or hate them, low-rise jeans are back, but Sweeney’s fall wardrobe is proof that we don’t need to wear them as if we teleported back in time. Take a cue from Sweeney and make the revival your own. Keep scrolling to discover some of the actress’ favorite American Eagle fall picks.

title: Beautycon Could Be The IRL Event You Need For Making Friends As An Adult
text:
Beautycon Could Be The IRL Event You Need For Making Friends As An Adult

Whether you’ve landed in a new city, started a new job or simply want to meet some new, interesting girlies, making friends as an adult is hard — for everyone. Add into the mix that it feels like we’re all more “chronically online” than ever before, so it is any wonder then that forging new friendships right now can feel like facing an impossible feat? Fear not — at Refinery29 we’ve been hyping up the need for IRL events (hello, Club R29!) for this very reason for quite some time now.  

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Beautycon (@beautycon)

So, mark your calendars, and prepare to make some new friends, because Beautycon is back in LA for another year. On September 19th, 2026, for one day only, the R29 team — and lots of incredible guests — will be enrolling everyone who comes along at Beautycon University at Rolling Greens. Just like the first day of school, it’ll be filled with new names and faces, so what better way to make some new friends? In case you haven’t heard, community-maxxing is in, and doomscrolling is out. 
 
Why now, you ask? “On an average day in 2023 one in 10 US young adults did not spend a single minute interacting face-to-face with another person,” the Financial Times reported earlier this year. Gen Z has been branded the ‘loneliest generation’ and millennials are constantly wondering why they can’t make more friends in their 30s — but there’s a change afoot because, according to our own reporting at R29, we’re seeing an uptick in women joining book clubs. Not to mention, women are seeking out new connections through hiking groups and/or a shared love of baking cakes. In short: women want to change this by finding their community through in-person events in the age of AI. So, if you love all things beauty then you may just find your people at our next event.  
 
People who love Cardi B, Keke Palmer and Sir John. That’s right; they’ve signed up and enrolled. Singer Cardi B will be bringing her Grow-Good beauty line to campus, and make-up artist Sir John will be our Head of School. To put it simply, we’ll all learn together. It’ll be filled with masterclasses, founder panels, and the brands you haven’t heard of but definitely need to know about. Just like university, you’ll also get to pick your own major — fun! You’ll learn in the classroom, and from creators onstage, and even get to try out some products, too.  

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Beautycon (@beautycon)

So, instead of downloading a friendship app yet again, pop along with your ticket in-hand and enroll yourself at Beautycon University. You never know who you might meet on your first — and only — day on campus.  

Beautycon will take place on September 19th, 2026, in LA. You can buy Beautycon tickets here.
